newsitem.title: MEXICO: Drugs seen as key issue in U.S.-Mexico talks.
newsitem.headline: Drugs seen as key issue in U.S.-Mexico talks.

text.p: The United States will focus on cooperation to combat drug trafficking and illegal immigration during top-level talks with Mexico next week, U.S. ambassador to Mexico James Jones said on Wednesday.
President Bill Clinton is scheduled to arrive in Mexico on Monday afternoon for his first official visit here.
Other issues in the meetings will be environmental concerns, transportation and customs specifications for Mexican agricultural exports, Jones added.
Mexico earlier on Wednesday announced a new drug fighting agency to replace the scandal-riddled National Institute for Drug Combat.
"I think Mexico has a strong commitment to win this fight," Jones said in an online news conference called to herald the launch of the embassy's new website (http://www.usembassy.org.mx).
"All of this is not to say that either Mexico or the U.S. is satisfied. There's still much more to do in both countries in order to be able to declare success against the menace of illegal drugs."

Mexican officials are also expected to share their concerns over tough new immigration measures put into effect recently in the United States. Mexican president Ernesto Zedillo has been pressured by opposition parties to address the issue with Clinton.

Jones said he did not foresee any talk of changing the three-year-old North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) which brought down trade and investment barriers between the United States, Canada and Mexico.
"I believe NAFTA has been a success in all areas...and will continue without change to the benefit of our two, three countries," Jones said.

Among the possible trade issues in the meetings are the delayed opening of the U.S. border to Mexican trucks, tariffs on Mexican cement and steel, the U.S. embargo on Mexican tuna and other ongoing agricultural trade disputes.
"I expect that many of these pending disagreements will be resolved in the Binational Commission meetings next week," Jones said.
The Binational Commission, a kind of annual joint U.S.-Mexico cabinet meeting to address major issues, is to meet on Monday just before Clinton arrives.
Clinton is also scheduled to tour the pre-Columbian Teotihuacan pyramids outside Mexico City and visit the historic colonial town of Tlaxcala.
Embassy officials said the list of secretaries to accompany Clinton had still had not been confirmed, but 13 U.S. cabinet members were scheduled to attend.

Among those expected were U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno, Energy Secretary Federico Pena, Commerce Secretary William Daley, drug czar Barry McCaffrey and Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, a U.S. embassy spokeswoman said.
